title: Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreements: A Geometric Perspective

elements.name: Two-stage GBALD framework
elements.description: GBALD integrates core-set construction (Stage 1) and model uncertainty estimation (Stage 2) into a unified active learning framework. Stage 1 constructs a core-set on an ellipsoid geometry to initialize representative acquisitions. Stage 2 uses MC dropout to rank batch acquisitions by informativeness and select the most representative ones.
elements.source_text: Our key technical innovation is to construct core-set on ellipsoid, not typical sphere, preventing low-representative elements from boundary distribution. Our work proposes a two-stage framework from a Bayesian perspective that sequentially introduces the core-set representation and model uncertainty estimation.

elements.name: MC dropout for Bayesian inference
elements.description: GBALD uses Monte Carlo dropout to approximate Bayesian inference on the neural network model. Multiple forward passes with dropout enabled produce a distribution over predictions, enabling estimation of predictive entropy and mutual information (BALD score).
elements.source_text: We follow 1 and use MC dropout to perform Bayesian inference on the neural network model. It then leads to ranking the informative acquisitions with batch sequences is with high efficiency.

elements.name: BALD dual interpretation
elements.description: BALD has two interpretations: (1) model uncertainty estimation -- selecting data that maximizes the decrease in expected posterior entropy, equivalent to maximizing mutual information between predictions and parameters; (2) core-set construction -- approximating the complete data posterior by a sparse subset via geodesic search.
elements.source_text: BALD has two different interpretations: model uncertainty estimation and core-set construction. ... maximizing the information gain in terms of predictive entropy over the model, and it is called Bayesian active learning by disagreements (BALD).

elements.name: Uninformative prior limitation
elements.description: When the initial labeled set D_0 has insufficient or unbalanced labels, the prior p(D_0 | theta) becomes uninformative. This causes BALD to produce biased, redundant acquisitions concentrated in few classes.
elements.source_text: an unbalanced label initialization on D_0 usually leads to an uninformative prior, which further conducts the acquisitions of AL to select those unlabeled data from one or some fixed classes; highly-biased results with redundant information are inevitable.

elements.name: Ellipsoid core-set construction
elements.description: Instead of spherical geodesic search for core-set construction, GBALD uses ellipsoid geometry by applying an affine rescaling factor eta (0 < eta < 1). This prevents updates from converging to boundary regions where data is less representative.
elements.source_text: Ellipsoid geodesic rescales the sphere geodesic to prevent the updates of core-set towards the boundary regions of the sphere where characteristics of spherical distribution cannot be properly captured.

elements.name: BALD acquisition score
elements.description: The BALD score selects x* that maximizes the decrease in expected posterior entropy, i.e., the mutual information between predictions and parameters. This is the core acquisition criterion used in Stage 2 of GBALD.
elements.source_text: x* = arg max_{x in D_u} H[theta|D_0] - E_{y ~ p(y|x,D_0)} [H[theta|x,y,D_0]]
elements.pseudocode: bald_score(x) = prior_entropy - E_y[predictive_entropy(x, y)] where prior_entropy = H[p(y|x, D_0)] and predictive_entropy = sum_y p(y|x,theta) * log(p(y|x,theta))

elements.name: Complete data log posterior
elements.description: Derives the expected complete data log posterior: E_y[log p(theta|D_0, x*, y*)] = log p(theta|D_0) + sum_i (E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]]). This is the theoretical foundation for core-set construction.
elements.source_text: E_{y*}[log p(theta|D_0, x*, y*)] = log p(theta|D_0) + sum_{i=1}^{N} (E_{y_i}[log p(y_i|x_i,theta) + H[y_i|x_i,D_0]])

elements.name: Core-set construction objective
elements.description: Core-set construction minimizes the L2 norm between the full log-likelihood L and the weighted log-likelihood L(w), selecting a sparse subset that approximates the complete data posterior.
elements.source_text: min_w || L - L(w) ||^2, where L = sum_i E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]] and L(w) = sum_i w_i E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]]
elements.pseudocode: loss = || sum_i E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]] - sum_i w_i * E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]] ||^2

elements.name: k-centers max-min selection
elements.description: The k-centers approach selects the data point tilde_x whose minimum distance to the current labeled set D_0 is maximal, using a greedy strategy independent of a trained discriminative model.
elements.source_text: tilde_x = argmax_{xi in D_u} min_{ci in D_0} ||xi - ci||
elements.pseudocode: x_tilde = argmax over xi in D_u of ( min over ci in D_0 of ||xi - ci|| )

elements.name: Geometric prior probability model
elements.description: Defines the initial probability p(yi|xi,theta) based on distance to the nearest labeled center Dj with radius R_0. If xi is within R_0 of any Dj, probability is 1; otherwise it is R_0 / ||xi - Dj||. This provides an informative geometric prior independent of a trained DNN.
elements.source_text: p(yi|xi,theta) = 1 if exists j such that ||xi - Dj|| <= R_0; max{R_0 / ||xi - Dj||} otherwise, for all j where ||xi - Di|| > R_0
elements.pseudocode: p(yi|xi, theta) = 1.0 if min_j ||xi - Dj|| <= R0 else R0 / min_j ||xi - Dj||

elements.name: Entropy approximation
elements.description: Approximates the joint entropy of outputs over the unlabeled pool using the geometric prior, enabling computation without a trained DNN.
elements.source_text: sum_i H(yi | xi, D_0) approx -sum_i p(yi|xi,theta) * log(p(yi|xi,theta))

elements.name: Likelihood constraint with k-means centers
elements.description: Constrains the log-likelihood L by an unbiased full likelihood L_0 computed over k-means centers U of the full input space X. Minimizes ||L_0 - L||^2 to prevent bias from the initial D_0.
elements.source_text: min_{x*} ||L_0 - L||^2, s.t. D_0 = D_0 union {x*, y*}, D_u = D_u \ x*
elements.pseudocode: L_0 = |sum_i E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,U]]|; loss = ||L_0 - L||^2

elements.name: Max-min weighted likelihood
elements.description: The max-w sub-optimizer for the core-set construction, which simplifies to sum_i w_i * log p(yi|xi,theta) * (1 - log p(yi|xi,theta)). Setting w_i=1 yields the unbiased form.
elements.source_text: max_{1<=i<=N} min_{w_i} sum_i w_i E_yi[log p(yi|xi,theta) + H[yi|xi,D_0]] = sum_i w_i * log p(yi|xi,theta) * (1 - log p(yi|xi,theta))

elements.name: Core-set acquisition criterion
elements.description: Combines the likelihood constraint and the max-min selection into a unified acquisition criterion for initial core-set construction. Selects x* that maximizes the sum of the likelihood regularization ||L_0 - L||^2 and the log-probability term log p(yj|xj,theta).
elements.source_text: x* = argmax_{xj in D_u} min_{Dj in D_0} { ||L_0 - L||^2 + log p(yj|xj,theta) }
elements.pseudocode: x_star = argmax over xj in D_u of ( min over Dj in D_0 of ( ||L_0 - L||^2 + log p(yj|xj,theta) ) )

elements.name: Ellipsoid geodesic rescaling
elements.description: The ellipsoid geodesic line rescales the sphere geodesic update. Given previous acquisition xi and next desired acquisition x*, the rescaled position is x*_e = xi + eta * (x* - xi), then mapped to the nearest unlabeled neighbor. The affine factor eta (0 < eta < 1) controls how far updates proceed toward distribution boundaries.
elements.source_text: x*_e = xi + eta(x* - xi), then argmin_{xj in D_u} ||xj - x*_e||
elements.pseudocode: x_e = xi + eta * (x_star - xi); x_rescaled = argmin over xj in D_u of ||xj - x_e||

elements.name: Batch BALD returns
elements.description: Rewrites the BALD criterion for batch returns: selects a batch of b candidates that maximize the expected posterior entropy decrease. Used in Stage 2 to return b informative acquisitions at once.
elements.source_text: {x_1*, ..., x_b*} = argmax_{x_hat_1:b in D_u} { H[theta|D_0] - E_{y_hat_1:b ~ p(y_hat_1:b | x_hat_1:b, D_0)} [H[theta|x_hat_1:b, y_hat_1:b, D_0]] }
elements.pseudocode: candidates = argmax over batches of size b from D_u of (prior_entropy - E_y[predictive_entropy])

elements.name: Representativeness ranking criterion
elements.description: Among the b BALD-ranked candidates, selects the one with the highest geometric representativeness using the geometric prior probability. x_t* = argmax over x_i* in the ranked batch of (max over Dj in D_0 of p(yi|xi*,theta)). This prevents selecting nearby/duplicate samples.
elements.source_text: x_t* = argmax_{xi* in {x_1*,...,x_b*}} { max_{Dj in D_0} p(yi|xi*,theta) := R_0 / ||xi* - Dj|| }
elements.pseudocode: x_t_star = argmax over xi_star in candidates of ( max over Dj in D_0 of R_0 / ||xi_star - Dj|| )

elements.name: Batch output selection
elements.description: Extends the single acquisition to a batch of b' outputs by selecting the b' candidates with the highest geometric representativeness probabilities from the b ranked acquisitions.
elements.source_text: {x_t1*, ..., x_tb'*} = argmax_{x_t1:tb'* subset of {x_1*,...,x_b*}} p(y_t1:tb'* | x_t1:tb'*, theta)
elements.pseudocode: batch_output = top k=b' candidates from ranked batch by p(yi|xi*, theta)

elements.name: Two-stage GBALD algorithm
elements.description: The complete GBALD algorithm. Stage 1 (Lines 3-13): constructs an initial core-set M using max-min optimization with ellipsoid geodesic search, initializing theta as a geometric probability model and k-means centers. Stage 2 (Lines 14-21): initializes theta as a DNN, iteratively returns b BALD-scored candidates, ranks b' most representative ones, and updates D_0 until budget A is exhausted.
elements.source_text: Input: Data set X, core-set size N_M, batch returns b, batch output b', iteration budget A. Stage 1: Initialize theta to yield geometric probability model. Perform k-means to initialize U. For i=1 to N_M: acquire x_i* using Eq (10), rescale with ellipsoid geodesic Eq (11), add to core-set M. Import core-set to update D_0. Stage 2: Initialize theta as DNN. While alpha < A: return b BALD acquisitions, rank b' most representative, update D_0.
elements.pseudocode:
Stage 1 (Core-set on ellipsoid):
  Initialize theta for geometric prior (Eq 5)
  U = k-means centers of D_u
  For i = 1 to N_M:
    x*_i = argmax over x in D_u of (min over Dj in D_0 of {||L_0 - L||^2 + log p(y|x,theta)})
    x*_i = ellipsoid_rescale(x*_i, previous_x, eta)  # Eq 11
    M = M union {x*_i}
  D_0 = M union nearest samples of U

Stage 2 (Model uncertainty estimation):
  Initialize DNN model with D_0
  While alpha < A:
    candidates = top b by BALD score from D_u  # Eq 12
    selected = top b' by representativeness from candidates  # Eq 14
    D_0 = D_0 union selected
    alpha += b'

elements.name: Tighter lower error bound with ellipsoid
elements.description: The lower bound of generalization error for geodesic search with ellipsoid is strictly less than that with sphere: lower[err(h,k)]_Ellipsoid < lower[err(h,k)]_Sphere. This means ellipsoid provides a tighter (more constraining) bound.
elements.source_text: Given a perceptron function h and sampling budget k, the lower bounds of geodesic search with sphere and ellipsoid satisfy: lower[err(h,k)]_Ellipsoid < lower[err(h,k)]_Sphere.

elements.name: Higher zero-error probability with ellipsoid
elements.description: The probability of achieving zero classification error with ellipsoid geodesic search is higher than with sphere: Pr[err(h,k)=0]_Ellipsoid > Pr[err(h,k)=0]_Sphere.
elements.source_text: the probabilities of geodesic search with sphere and ellipsoid satisfy: Pr[err(h,k) = 0]_Ellipsoid > Pr[err(h,k) = 0]_Sphere.

elements.name: Theorem 1: Sphere geodesic error bound
elements.description: Provides upper and lower bounds on the classification error err(h,k) for geodesic search with sphere. The lower bound involves radii Ra, Rb and tk. Upper bound is 1/k.

elements.name: Theorem 2: Ellipsoid geodesic error bound
elements.description: Provides the error bound for ellipsoid geodesic search, analogous to Theorem 1 but using ellipsoid radii (Ra_1, Ra_2, Ra_3). Shows a tighter lower bound than the sphere case.
elements.source_text: min{ (4 prod Ra_i - (2Ra_1 + Lk)(Ra_1 - Lk)^2) / (4 prod Ra_i + 4 prod Rb_i), ... } < err(h,k) < 1/k

elements.name: Theorem 3: Volume generalization to hypersphere
elements.description: Shows that the volume of a 3-D sphere is a low-dimensional generalization of the d-dimensional hypersphere through recursive integral operations.
elements.source_text: Vol_d(S_a) can be approximated by integrating over (d-1)-dimensional hyperspheres, establishing Vol_d(S_a) bowtie Vol_3(S_a) as a low-dimensional generalization.

elements.name: Theorem 4: Volume generalization to hyperellipsoid
elements.description: Shows that the volume of a 3-D ellipsoid is a low-dimensional generalization of the d-dimensional hyperellipsoid, extending Theorems 1-2 to arbitrary dimensions.
elements.source_text: Vol_d(E_a) can be generalized from 3-D ellipsoid through recursive integral operations, with 3-D ellipsoid volume as the low-dimensional generalization.

elements.name: GBALD hyperparameter defaults
elements.description: Default hyperparameter values used in experiments: R_0 = 2.0e+3 (geometric prior radius), eta = 0.9 (ellipsoid afffine factor), MC dropout samples = 2000, batch returns b = 300 for batch mode / b = 3 for single acquisition mode, batch output b' = 100 for batch mode / b' = 1 for single acquisition mode.
elements.source_text: The parameter settings of Eq. (5) are R_0 = 2.0e + 3 and eta = 0.9. We use 2,000 MC dropout samples from the unlabeled data pool. For single acquisition of GBALD, we suggest b=3 and b'=1. For batch acquisitions, GBALD ranks b=300 acquisitions to select b'=100 data for training.

elements.name: Core-set size N_M
elements.description: The core-set size N_M controls how many initial samples are drawn via ellipsoid geodesic construction before Stage 2 begins. Table 6 shows performance for N_M in {1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000} on SVHN. Performance is stable for N_M >= 1000, optimal at N_M = 5000 for start accuracy.
elements.source_text: Table 6 presents the relationship of accuracies and size of core-set, where start accuracy denotes the test accuracy over the initial core-set, and ultimate accuracy denotes the test accuracy over up to Q=20,000 training data. The GBALD algorithm keeps stable accuracies when there are inputs more than 1,000 core-set labels.

elements.name: Iteration budget A
elements.description: The iteration budget A = (Q - N_M) / b' controls the number of Stage 2 rounds given total acquisition budget Q, core-set size N_M, and batch output size b'.
elements.source_text: Given the acquisition budget Q, let b' be the number of the output returns at each loop, N_M be the number of the core-set size, the iteration budget A of GBALD then can be defined as A = (Q - N_M) / b'.

elements.name: Uninformative prior experiment
elements.description: Tests how BALD degrades under uninformative prior (initialized from single class). Compares BALD with various batch sizes (1, 10, 20, 30, 40) against GBALD on MNIST digits '0' and '1'. GBALD outperforms all BALD variants by using core-set to provide complete label coverage from the start.
elements.source_text: Based on the uninformative setting of p(D_0|theta), we randomly select 20 samples from digit '0' and '1' to initialize D_0. BALD with Batchsize=10 shows better performance than that of Batchsize=1; while in Figure 3(a) BALD keeps stable performance. Different to BALD, core-set construction of GBALD provides a complete label matching against all classes.

elements.name: Improved informative acquisitions experiment
elements.description: Compares BALD vs GBALD with different batch sizes (b in {3, 5, 7}, b'=1) on MNIST to demonstrate how GBALD's ranking reduces redundancy. GBALD outperforms BALD even as the ranked batch size increases.
elements.source_text: we compare the best performance of BALD with a batch size of 1 and GBALD with different batch size parameters. Following Eq. (14), we set b = {3, 5, 7} and b'=1. BALD cannot accelerate the model as fast as GBALD due to the repeated information over the acquisitions. GBALD significantly outperforms BALD, even if we progressively increase the ranked batch size b.

elements.name: Active acquisitions benchmark
elements.description: Main benchmark comparing GBALD against Var, BALD, Entropy, k-medoids, and k-centers on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10. Uses a 3-layer MLP with MC dropout. GBALD (b=300, b'=100) achieves highest mean accuracy across all three datasets.
elements.source_text: The batch size of the compared baselines is 100, where GBALD ranks 300 acquisitions to select 100 data for the training, i.e. b = 300, b' = 100. GBALD achieves the highest average accuracies on all three datasets.

elements.name: Repeated samples robustness experiment
elements.description: Tests robustness against repeated samples in SVHN. Adds 5000 or 10000 repeated samples and measures GBALD vs Var and BALD. GBALD shows slighter perturbations due to core-set initialization.
elements.source_text: we compare the acquisition performance of BALD, Var, and GBALD using 5,000 and 10,000 repeated samples from the SVHN dataset. GBALD shows slighter perturbations on the repeated samples than Var and BALD because it draws the core-set from the input distribution as the initial acquisitions.

elements.name: Noisy labels robustness experiment
elements.description: Tests robustness against label noise. 5000 or 10000 samples in MNIST have their labels shifted by 1. Compares GBALD vs Var and BALD on SVHN. GBALD has smaller accuracy degradation.
elements.source_text: we select the first 5,000 and 10,000 samples respectively from the unlabeled data pool of the MNIST dataset and reset their labels by shifting {'0', '1',...,'8'} to {'1', '2',...,'9'}. GBALD has smaller noisy perturbations than the other baselines.

elements.name: GBALD vs BatchBALD comparison
elements.description: Compares GBALD against BatchBALD with various batch sizes (10, 40, 100) on MNIST. BatchBALD degrades with larger batch sizes while GBALD maintains high performance. GBALD has much higher mean accuracy across all settings.
elements.source_text: BatchBALD degenerates the test accuracies if we progressively increase the batch sizes, where BatchBALD with a batch size of 10 keeps similar learning curves as BALD. The statistical results show that GBALD has much higher mean accuracy than BatchBALD with different batch sizes.

elements.name: Core-set size sensitivity
elements.description: Studies how core-set size N_M affects GBALD performance on SVHN. Tests N_M in {1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000} with fixed b=1000, b'=500. Performance is stable for N_M >= 1000.
elements.source_text: Table 6 presents the relationship of accuracies and size of core-set. The GBALD algorithm keeps stable accuracies when there inputs more than 1,000 core-set labels.

elements.name: Statistical significance t-test
elements.description: Two-sided t-test on learning curve breakpoints to establish statistical significance. Computes pairwise penalty matrix showing GBALD has significant superiority over all baselines on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10.
elements.source_text: We present two-sided t-test for the learning curves. t-score = sqrt(n) * mu / sigma, where mu = (1/n) sum_i (alpha_i - beta_i). Column-wise values at the bottom of each matrix show overall performance. GBALD has significant performance over the three datasets.
elements.pseudocode: t_score = sqrt(n) * mu / sigma; where mu = mean(alpha_i - beta_i), sigma = std(alpha_i - beta_i - mu)
